title: Joan Memorial
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: In this Soto Zen dharma talk, Nomon Tim Burnett shares personal stories about their family members' experiences with illness and loss, highlighting the importance of being present with loved ones in the end stages of life. They reflect on how these experiences have taught them that life is precious and fleeting, and that relationships with others are essential to our well-being. Nomon encourages listeners to cultivate forgiveness, understanding, and appreciation for those who help us, while also finding hope and positivity in the midst of grief and loss.

sentences.text: Nice to be back amongst you all, good friends.
I was away traveling the first half of April, and then this last week I was called away to help with a family health crisis, which turned out to be a family death.
Joan Burnett was my stepmother, but the relationship is a little more complicated than that, because she's also the mother of my stepbrother.
See if you can figure that out.
I'll explain.
It's like those jokes where your grandfather is the son of your father.
This is a koan.
Yeah, it's a koan.
Joan has been a part of my life since I was a baby, actually, or at least very young.
Joan and my father were married in 1976, but they were very close for some years before that.
I don't usually talk about this part of my family history because it sounds a little strange, but actually it worked out pretty well for everybody.
My birth parents, who are called Toby and Nita, were really close to another family.
Often families have another family that you're close to.
The parents in the other family were named Joan and Ed.
Both couples had kids, and both had two boys, and the two boys were about the same age, [unclear: "which brother was"].
And my sister was younger.
We were living a few blocks from each other in San Diego, where Toby and Ed were graduate students in physics.
And the families got really close.
After a while, and of course we didn't know this until many years later, it became clear to both couples that they had married the wrong person.
But everybody agreed, somehow.
I don't know how the communication happened initially.
And apparently my father's been sharing some of these details with my sister, so maybe I'll find out.
The two couples agreed that they had married the wrong person and that the logical thing to do was to be with the other person.
And so Toby and Joan got close, and Nita and Ed got close.
Initially they didn't want to divorce or mess things up with the kids, so they were just kind of doing this on the sly.
They were pretty conventional-looking people, but it was the late 60s, early 70s.
Everybody was happy, and love is love.
But eventually it couldn't last.
The couples did get divorced and remarried in 1975-76.
And actually for Joan and my father, for Toby and Joan, and for my mother and Ed, Nita and Ed, they more or less lived happily ever after.
Not that divorce and the re-scrambling of families wasn't really hard on the kids, the five kids, it really was.
I didn't realize for years how angry I was about all this happening to me.
Especially because in the end we did not live two blocks from each other.
My dad got a job in Seattle, and Ed did not get a job in Seattle.
So one couple took a couple of kids and the other couple took a couple of kids and ended up in two different states.
And so I didn't see my father very much for the rest of my upbringing.
He would mostly fly in for work, take a couple of hours, and take us to miniature golf.
At least that's what I remember.
I don't remember doing anything other than miniature golf, maybe pizza: miniature golf and pizza.
And he actually told my sister yesterday how sorry he was that that's what happened.
I don't think he tried to explain it, but I think I get it.
He just somehow thought he would see us all the time anyway, even though he lived in a different state.
And he was a very smart, overachieving, late 20s guy.
People had kids young.
And I think he just didn't really think about it that much until a decade later, when he realized, well, I didn't really see my kids that much.
What happened?
He was busy and successful with his work.
At least it went on pretty happily for both couples until the end of February of this year, when Joan had a bad flu and some dizziness, and she fell in the bathroom.
Janet and I were in the house, actually, when she fell in the bathroom.
She [unclear: "had talus"] for a couple hours.
And then eventually she was coughing up blood and realized she really better go to the doctor.
Maybe this just wasn't the flu.
The wonder of modern diagnostics and scans and stuff, Ken knows about this I guess, is that they could tell her within a couple of hours: well, we're really sorry.
No, you don't have the flu.
You have stage four lung cancer and it's not treatable.
It's only treatable for quality of life, but it's fatal.
Can you imagine in one evening going from "this is a bad flu" to "oh, my life is ending"?
And of course it happens much more quickly than that for many people.
Then after a big flurry of medical appointments and shock and sorrow, she seemed to be responding to treatments such that maybe she would live for at least a while.
She did a few rounds of radiation, was feeling much better, finished her taxes.
She was really worried that she would not be able to take care of the taxes.
And my dad went off on a work trip, some work that was very important to him, figuring everything was okay for now.
Maybe they could travel, he said, go to some of their favorite places while she still was able to.
And then she started coughing, really intense coughing.
Apparently, I wasn't there, but continuous hacking coughs.
Her sister was visiting and staying with her and took her back to the doctor.
And they very quickly found out, no, that's not just a cough.
You have a serious pneumonia in the other lung, and we've got to admit you to the hospital and put you on a breathing machine.
It looked like she might be able to recover from that.
They didn't know what was causing the pneumonia, so they treat it for everything, I guess is what they usually do: broad spectrum antibiotics and fluids and a way of feeding her.
But she wasn't able to recover from the pneumonia.
A week later, she had no lung function left and was just living by virtue of a respirator machine and intubation.
I don't know if we ever found out what caused the pneumonia, but the most likely theory was a fungus, which is in the environment anyway.
We're probably breathing a few spores of it right now.
PCP, I think it's called, initials for the Latin name.
But if your immune system is compromised and your lungs are a mess, it's a whole different story.
So last Tuesday we gathered in her hospital room.

My immediate family had seen her the previous Sunday when she was just on a breath machine, kind of like a CPAP that people have for sleep problems, just a more intense version called a BiPAP, I think.
So she was still conscious and could still talk a little, but you couldn't hear her through the mask.
By the time we got back there on Tuesday, she had lost consciousness.
Instead of just a mask, it was a tube down her throat and a conventional respirator machine doing all the breathing.
My dad was there.
My brother Brad flew up for the day.
My sister Carla came immediately.
I was really amazed, actually.
She's had a lot of issues with my dad because she was so young when all the scrambling happened.
She never felt like she got what she needed.

But when I emailed my brother and sister and said, I don't want to be the negative guy, but I think it's really serious and you might want to get on a plane, the reply half an hour later was her plane reservation.
It was amazing.
So Carla, my sister, was there all week.
Joan's surviving son Jeff and Jeff's wife Melissa were there.
We stood in a circle around the hospital bed listening to the breathing machine, looking at Joan in her hospital gown, eyes closed, face a little puffy.
Because of the tube, her mouth and eyes were a little bit open.
There was a real deep beauty to the moment, this moment of being with somebody right at the end, but it also wasn't very pretty.
So beautiful, but not pretty.
Once everyone was there and we had a little minute to collect ourselves, we gave the signal to the nurse and the respiration specialist came in.
His name was Enrico.
He was the sweetest guy.
I was trying to imagine having this job, where a big part of your job is to do what he had to do in that moment.
He came in very tenderly.
His eyes were soft, his movements were slow and careful.
He told Joan each thing he was doing as he removed the different tubes and plugs and prepared to take the main tube out of her throat.
He had a little hand respirator thing, so he gave her a few breaths during the process.
He just had a real feeling of kindness and connection.
He really felt like he was in a very connected, warm relationship with this patient.
And he had seen her over the week that she was there as well and had put the tube in too.
So Enrico did his work.
They took all the tubes and IV lines out and they withdrew.
I don't know if they had some way of monitoring us or what, but all the monitors were off of Joan and they gave us as much space as we needed.
Once the machine was off, her body still wanted to breathe, even though the lungs weren't really doing anything.
Short breaths, spaced far apart, and over time less and less frequent.
My dad was sobbing and talking to her, cradling her head, holding her hand.
My sister and I took turns just being in physical contact with my dad, a hand on his shoulder.
My brother had to turn away for a few minutes, but then he was able to turn back.
My stepbrother was really quiet, very still, watching as his mother left this life.
There were a few last minutes when we thought that had been the last breath.
A long pause, and then one more breath.
The body just so wants to keep living.
And yet the conditions that support life, that allow life to keep going, are so fragile.
Such a reminder of that reality.
A few cells went haywire.
One of the many systems wasn't working quite right.
Ordinary things in the air and in the water that are ready for an opening in the system.
From our point of view, we're living beings and individuals.
But from another point of view, maybe of a virus or a fungus, we're actually a place to live.
We are habitat.
From the Buddhist perspective, being born as a human being is seen as a really precious opportunity.
That's our time for practice among the many lifetimes in the cosmological Buddhist scheme, which has many lifetimes and many levels of many worlds.
This being human is our time for connection, for practice, and for love.
And the reminder is that it's a pretty short window.
Brief.
The flapping of a butterfly's wings is one of the analogies.
That's how long human life is, one flapping of a butterfly's wings.
One of the traditional ways to contemplate this is a verse called the Five Remembrances.
Here's [unclear: "Thidna Han's"] version.
We don't have this regularly in our liturgy, but maybe we should.
*The Five Remembrances are, I am of a nature to grow old.
There is no way to escape growing old.
I am of a nature to have ill health.
There is no way to escape ill health.
I am of a nature to die.
There is no way to escape death.
All that is dear to me and everyone I love are of a nature to change.
There is no way to escape being separated from them.
My actions are my only true belongings.
My actions are my only true belongings.
I cannot escape the consequence of my actions, and my actions are the ground upon which I stand.*
So I'll tell you a little bit about Joan's actions.
Joan was all about supporting other people.
She was also supportive of me as a practitioner and actually of our Sangha.
She gave us several significant donations on her and my dad's behalf.
She really liked my essays in the email newsletter, the Responding Gate newsletter.
We never really would talk about it.
As far as I know, she wasn't interested in meditation for herself.
But one time I was really surprised that she had taken one of those essays and edited it.
I write them pretty fast, so there are usually a few typos.
She cleaned it up, edited the typos, and actually made some edits for clarity and read it out loud to my grandmother, who was having trouble reading.
I was so touched by that.
And the same grandmother was a great inspiration to me, spiritually, actually.
For work, Joan was a social worker, an MSW social worker, mostly working with families in bad straights in our society.
She did a lot of work for the state, helping people to set up home daycares, how to do that safely, so the kids would be well cared for.
But then in the early 90s, her younger son, Mark, at age 23, died.
He had a friend who was a small plane pilot, a buddy.
They went on a flying trip to see the tulips in Skagit Valley.
Some kind of strange environmental event happened, and the plane fell out of the sky, and they died instantly.
So the tulip festival has always been an important time in our family life, and now Joan herself is also dying during the tulip time.
When Mark died, it was really hard.
She stopped working.
She did skillful things to heal, joined support groups, but mostly she brought her great work of helping others home.
She focused a lot on supporting my dad.

It sounds a little cliché, but they did a sort of conventional division of labor at home, where she took care of the home life completely, more than conventional, not just the cooking and cleaning, but also the finances and the taxes and all the arrangements and the social planning, trip planning, supporting him so he could really just focus on his work.
And my dad actually ended up being an important figure in his field.
He's a world expert on the processing with computers of very large amounts of scientific data from physics, high energy physics, and astrophysics experiments.
I only found this out in little bits and pieces and didn't really talk that much about his work.
What I didn't realize, until Joan told me about her cancer diagnosis, was that she really saw her work as making my dad's work possible, in a very direct way.
She felt like she was contributing to science and to understanding the world, that it wasn't just bills and shopping and fretting, that it was actually important work.
The reason that became clear to me is the first thing she told me.
I talked to her the day after the diagnosis, and the first thing she told me was, "I have cancer in my lungs, I will not survive this, and it's very important that Toby continues his work."
That's the first thing she said.
And then that she was worried about her sister, then she was worried about the bills and the taxes.
She didn't really seem to have any concern about her own well-being.
Another very true cliché about death is that you don't know what you've got until it's gone.
So I think we really take the people who help and support others for granted.
And Joan actually wasn't all that easy to like at times.
A lot of her words and deeds and focus were about problems: worrying about problems, heading off problems, talking about problems, solving problems.
Staying one step ahead of all the possible pitfalls that might befall her and the people she was supporting.
So it was hard for the adjective "fussy" not to come to mind.
It was really hard to not give that word some weight in your mind.
But that was not seeing the forest for the trees, not seeing the people she was caring for, the cats she was caring for.
She had a great practice of taking in very sick cats from the shelter and taking care of them night and day until they died, which drove us a little nuts at times.
I'm sure the cats really, really appreciated it.
And also, so often the helpers are women, right?
And the doers out in front are men.
So may I learn from this.
So thank you, Joan.
Thank you for helping me and helping my father.
For caring for your children.
Thank you for surviving the loss of your son.
For caring for all those darn sick cats.
For being such an attentive grandmother.
It hasn't really sunk in with Walker yet that you're gone, but he'll mourn you in his own way over time.
And we're going to do our best to keep Dad afloat.
I'm so glad to tell you that he's not shutting down.
He's staying open.
Sobbing and laughing, and with the brightness that shines through all of it, he'll be okay.
He'll always miss you, but he'll continue his work and his life.
And he's excited to be a bigger part of the lives of his kids and grandkids.
So there's a good thing from all this.
